The Impett, Park & Muise critique is real, published in Current Directions in Psychological Science (2024, not 2022-2023 as the entry states). Their three core conclusions — no reliable primary language, no matching benefit, weak 5-factor structure — are well-supported. A 2017 couples study (Bunt & Hazelwood) found limited support for matching. Egbert & Polk (2006) found some psychometric support, so evidence is "mixed leaning negative" rather than fully null. The pop framing (stable primary language; matching predicts satisfaction) does NOT match the science. Keep the entry because (a) the cultural reach is huge and users will encounter it, (b) it's still defensible as a conversation prompt, and (c) the entry already takes a skeptical stance. Tighten the citation date and add the matching-study nuance.
inputs.revisedPitfalls: The popular framing does not match the science. A 2024 review by Impett, Park & Muise in Current Directions in Psychological Science concluded the model lacks empirical support on three fronts: (1) people don't reliably have a single stable "primary" love language — preferences shift by context, mood, and relationship phase; (2) couples whose top languages "match" do not consistently report higher relationship satisfaction (a 2017 couples study by Bunt & Hazelwood found only weak matching effects); (3) the five-category factor structure is poorly validated, with mixed psychometric results across studies. The authors argue lasting love depends on a broad, flexible repertoire of relational behaviors, not on hitting one preferred mode. Treat the five categories as a vocabulary for talking about preferences, not as a personality typology or diagnostic. Concrete risks: (a) using "that's not my love language" to refuse effort in modes you find harder, (b) treating your partner's preferences as fixed when they vary by situation, (c) substituting the quiz for actual specific conversation about what felt caring this week.

entries.name: Confirmation Bias
entries.oneLiner: We seek, remember, and weight evidence that confirms what we already believe, and discount what doesn't.
entries.description: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, and recall information in a way that supports prior beliefs. It is one of the most replicated findings in cognitive psychology and operates across politics, hiring, medical diagnosis, and investing. Critically, it is mostly unconscious; even experts who know about it still exhibit it.
entries.example: An investor convinced a stock will rise reads bullish analyst notes, dismisses the bearish quarterly report as 'noise,' and ends up holding through a 40% drawdown. A hiring manager who 'liked' a candidate in the first 30 seconds spends the rest of the interview asking questions whose answers fit that first impression.
entries.howToApply: Before a decision, write down what evidence would change your mind, then deliberately search for it. Steel-man the opposing view in writing. Use a pre-mortem: 'It's one year later and this decision failed. Why?' For high-stakes calls, assign a teammate the role of 'red-teamer' whose job is to argue the other side.
entries.pitfalls: Don't confuse it with simply having strong evidence; Bayesian updating still favors well-supported priors. Also: 'debiasing' training has weak transfer effects in the lab; structural fixes (checklists, blind review, pre-registration) outperform willpower.
entries.origin: Peter Wason, 1960 (2-4-6 rule-discovery task); concept popularized by Raymond Nickerson's 1998 review in Review of General Psychology.

entries.name: Survivorship Bias
entries.oneLiner: We study the winners and ignore the graveyard, drawing lessons from a sample that excludes failures.
entries.description: Survivorship bias occurs when analysis focuses only on entities that 'survived' some selection process, ignoring those that didn't, leading to overly optimistic conclusions. The classic illustration is Abraham Wald's WWII work on bomber armor: the planes that returned showed bullet holes in the wings and tail, but the Statistical Research Group correctly inferred the engines and cockpit needed armor because planes hit there didn't make it back.
entries.example: Reading 'how I built a $10M startup' Twitter threads as a playbook ignores the thousands of founders who followed identical advice and went bankrupt. Mutual fund rankings that only show currently-existing funds inflate average returns by 1-2% per year because closed/merged underperformers are deleted.
entries.howToApply: Before copying a strategy, ask: 'What's the base rate of failure for people who tried this?' Seek out failed cases explicitly (post-mortems, bankruptcy filings, abandoned-project blogs). When evaluating performance data, demand survivor-free databases (e.g., CRSP for stocks).
entries.pitfalls: Survivors sometimes really do have signal worth learning from, especially when the survival mechanism is skill rather than luck. The fix isn't to ignore winners but to also study comparable losers.
entries.origin: Statistical concept; named explicitly in finance/management literature in the 1990s. Wald's bomber analysis (Statistical Research Group, Columbia, 1943) is the canonical example.

entries.name: Anchoring
entries.oneLiner: The first number you see warps every subsequent estimate, even when it's obviously irrelevant.
entries.description: Anchoring is the tendency for an initial reference point to bias subsequent numerical judgments. In Tversky & Kahneman's original demonstration, a spun wheel of fortune showing 10 or 65 shifted participants' estimates of the percentage of African nations in the UN, even though everyone knew the wheel was random. Anchoring is one of the most replicable effects in behavioral economics.
entries.example: A house listed at $1.2M frames a $1.05M offer as a 'discount,' even if comparables suggest $950K is fair. A menu's $95 steak makes the $48 pasta seem reasonable. In salary negotiation, whoever names the first number typically captures more of the surplus.
entries.howToApply: Decide your reservation price and target before hearing the other side's number. When given an anchor, write down an independent estimate from first principles before responding. In negotiations, anchor first when you have good information; defer when you don't. For purchases, research comparable prices before exposure to the seller's number.
entries.pitfalls: Some 'anchoring' studies in priming research have failed to replicate, but the core numerical-anchoring effect is robust. Don't anchor aggressively when you're under-informed; an extreme anchor can blow up the deal or signal bad faith.
entries.origin: Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman, 1974, 'Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases,' Science 185:1124-1131.

entries.name: Availability Heuristic
entries.oneLiner: We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, not by actual frequency.
entries.description: The availability heuristic is a mental shortcut where probability is estimated by ease of recall. Vivid, recent, or emotionally charged events feel more probable than they are. It explains why people overestimate plane-crash and shark-attack risk, and underestimate cardiovascular disease (which kills ~1 in 4 Americans but rarely makes the front page).
entries.example: After watching a news cycle on a kidnapping, parents drive their kids to school, exposing them to a much higher per-mile fatality risk than the abduction they're avoiding. After a friend's startup IPO, you overestimate the probability that yours will too.
entries.howToApply: For any risk decision, look up base rates before reacting. Ask: 'Am I scared because the data says so, or because the example is vivid?' Maintain a 'boring statistics' bookmark folder (CDC, actuarial tables, BLS) for common decisions. Wait 24-48 hours before acting on news-driven emotional impulses.
entries.pitfalls: Availability sometimes tracks reality (frequent things really are more recallable). The bias is in the asymmetric weighting of vividness vs. frequency, not in memory-based reasoning per se.
entries.origin: Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman, 1973, 'Availability: A heuristic for judging frequency and probability,' Cognitive Psychology 5:207-232.

entries.name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
entries.oneLiner: We keep investing in losing courses because of what we've already spent, even though that money is gone either way.
entries.description: The sunk cost fallacy is continued commitment to an endeavor based on previously invested (and unrecoverable) resources, rather than expected future value. Rational decision theory says only marginal future costs and benefits should matter; humans systematically violate this. Concorde's continued funding despite known unprofitability is the textbook case ('Concorde fallacy').
entries.example: Sitting through a bad 3-hour movie because you already paid; staying in a 4-year relationship because you've 'invested 4 years'; finishing a graduate program you hate because you're 'already halfway through.' Companies pour another $50M into a doomed product because they've spent $200M.
entries.howToApply: Reframe every ongoing decision as: 'If I were starting fresh today with no history, would I begin this?' If no, exit. Set kill-criteria before starting projects ('I'll abandon this if X by month 6'). Separate the accountant's view (sunk costs are zero) from the storyteller's view (which protects ego).
entries.pitfalls: Sometimes 'persistence pays off' really is correct: if completing the project unlocks a step-function payoff (vesting, credentials, network effects), the marginal calculus may favor finishing. The fallacy is treating past spend itself as a reason; legitimate reasons are always forward-looking.
entries.origin: Concept formalized by Hal Arkes & Catherine Blumer, 1985, 'The Psychology of Sunk Cost,' Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 35:124-140.

entries.name: Hindsight Bias
entries.oneLiner: After an event, we remember having 'known it all along,' which corrupts how we learn from outcomes.
entries.description: Hindsight bias is the tendency, once an outcome is known, to overestimate how predictable it was beforehand. Fischhoff's classic studies showed people who learned an event's outcome reported they would have predicted it; people without the outcome rarely did. It distorts post-mortems, lawsuit verdicts, and personal regret.
entries.example: After a startup's IPO, founders' early bets seem 'obviously brilliant'; after its collapse, the same bets seem 'obviously stupid.' After 2008, every financial commentator 'saw the housing crash coming,' though contemporaneous predictions were mixed. Juries judging a doctor's pre-incident decisions know the bad outcome and rate the decision as more negligent.
entries.howToApply: Write down predictions with timestamps before outcomes are known (a 'forecasting journal' or tools like Manifold). In post-mortems, separate decision quality from outcome quality, judging the decision against what was knowable at the time. When evaluating others' past calls, ask: 'What did the consensus say then?'
entries.pitfalls: Don't overcorrect into 'no one could have known': sometimes warning signs really were available and ignored. The fix is documented foresight, not blanket forgiveness.
entries.origin: Baruch Fischhoff, 1975, 'Hindsight ≠ Foresight: The effect of outcome knowledge on judgment under uncertainty,' Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance 1:288-299.

entries.name: Loss Aversion
entries.oneLiner: Losses hurt roughly twice as much as equivalent gains feel good, distorting risk-taking.
entries.description: Loss aversion is the central asymmetry in Kahneman & Tversky's prospect theory: the disutility of losing $X is about 1.5-2.5x the utility of gaining $X. It explains the endowment effect, status-quo bias, and disposition effect (selling winners, holding losers). Recent meta-analyses (Gal & Rucker 2018; Mrkva et al. 2020) suggest the ~2x ratio is context-dependent and sometimes weaker, but the asymmetry itself is robust.
entries.example: Investors hold losing stocks too long ('I'll sell when it gets back to even') and sell winners too early. People reject a 50/50 bet to win $110 or lose $100 even though it's positive EV. Homeowners refuse to list below their purchase price even when comparable sales say they should.
entries.howToApply: Reframe in terms of total wealth, not gains/losses from a reference point ('Will I be richer in 5 years?'). Pre-commit to rules: stop-losses, automatic rebalancing, automatic 401(k) contributions. For sticky decisions, ask: 'If I didn't already own this, would I buy it today at the market price?' If not, sell.
entries.pitfalls: The popular '2:1' ratio is not a universal constant; it shrinks for small stakes, frequent decisions, and experienced traders. Don't use loss aversion to justify never taking risks; over a lifetime, excessive risk avoidance is itself a large hidden loss.
entries.origin: Daniel Kahneman & Amos Tversky, 1979, 'Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk,' Econometrica 47:263-291.

entries.name: Negativity Bias
entries.oneLiner: Bad is stronger than good: negative events grab more attention, weight, and memory than equivalent positives.
entries.description: Negativity bias is the asymmetric weighting of negative information across attention, learning, memory, and decisions. Baumeister et al.'s 'Bad is Stronger than Good' (2001) and Rozin & Royzman's 'Negativity Bias, Negativity Dominance, and Contagion' (2001) document this across domains: one criticism outweighs five compliments, one bad meal taints a restaurant's reputation, lost money hurts more than equal gains.
entries.example: A glowing performance review with one critical line: you ruminate on the criticism for a week. One bad Yelp review sinks a small restaurant despite 50 good ones. News feeds optimize for outrage because negative headlines drive more clicks per impression.
entries.howToApply: Use a 5:1 'positivity ratio' rule of thumb in feedback to others (Gottman's marriage research finds healthy couples run roughly 5:1 positive to negative interactions). Keep a daily 'three good things' log; meta-analyses (Bolier et al. 2013) find modest but real well-being effects. Audit your information diet: remove sources whose business model is anger.
entries.pitfalls: Don't suppress legitimate negative signals; pain and fear exist for good reasons. The Losada/Fredrickson '2.9013 ratio' was retracted as mathematically invalid (Brown, Sokal & Friedman 2013), and broad 'positive psychology' claims have a mixed replication record.
entries.origin: Roy Baumeister, Ellen Bratslavsky, Catrin Finkenauer, & Kathleen Vohs, 2001, 'Bad is Stronger than Good,' Review of General Psychology 5:323-370; concurrently Paul Rozin & Edward Royzman, 2001.

entries.name: Bandwagon Effect (Social Proof)
entries.oneLiner: We adopt beliefs and behaviors because others have, often without independent evaluation.
entries.description: The bandwagon effect is the tendency to do or believe things because many other people do. It overlaps with informational cascades (Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer & Welch 1992), where each person rationally infers from others' choices, leading the whole group to converge on possibly-wrong answers. Asch's 1951 conformity experiments demonstrated that ~37% of trials produced conformity to an obviously wrong group answer.
entries.example: Meme stocks (GameStop 2021, AMC), crypto bubbles, and Beanie Babies all show price detached from fundamentals because each new buyer infers value from prior buyers. In meetings, once two people endorse an idea, dissent drops sharply. Restaurant queues attract more queuers regardless of food quality.
entries.howToApply: Before adopting a popular position, write down your independent reasoning first, then update on the crowd. In meetings, collect anonymous written opinions before discussion (a 'Delphi' approach) to prevent cascades. Ask: 'Do these people have private information, or are they following each other?' If the latter, the crowd carries less signal than it appears.
entries.pitfalls: Crowds are sometimes right (wisdom of crowds requires diverse, independent estimates per Surowiecki/Galton). The fallacy is treating popularity as evidence; the corrective is diversity and independence of the sources, not contrarianism for its own sake.
entries.origin: Term from 19th-century U.S. politics (Dan Rice, 1848 campaign for Zachary Taylor); experimentally formalized by Solomon Asch, 1951; cascade theory by Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer & Welch, 1992.

entries.name: Recency Bias
entries.oneLiner: We overweight what happened recently and assume it will continue, ignoring longer-run base rates.
entries.description: Recency bias is the tendency to give disproportionate weight to recent events when forecasting or judging. It's related to the availability heuristic but specifically about temporal proximity. In memory research, it shows up as the 'recency effect' in serial recall (Murdock 1962); in forecasting, it manifests as extrapolating recent trends.
entries.example: After a strong year, retail investors pour money into the previous year's top-performing fund category, which historically reverts (DALBAR's annual studies estimate this 'behavior gap' at ~1-2% per year of underperformance). Managers rate employees mostly on the last month before review. After one bad date, you conclude you 'always pick wrong.'
entries.howToApply: For any forecast, look at 10+ years of history, not 1-2. Use rolling averages and base rates instead of point-in-time snapshots. For performance reviews, keep a running notes file for each report so the last two weeks don't dominate. In investing, set an asset allocation and rebalance on a calendar, not on news.
entries.pitfalls: Recent data sometimes really does carry the most signal (regime changes, structural breaks). The skill is asking whether the underlying generator has actually changed; if not, mean reversion usually wins.
entries.origin: Memory effect documented by Bennet Murdock, 1962, 'The serial position effect of free recall,' Journal of Experimental Psychology 64:482-488; decision-making applications throughout the heuristics-and-biases tradition (Kahneman, Slovic & Tversky 1982).

entries.name: Pareto Principle (80/20 Rule)
entries.oneLiner: Roughly 80% of outcomes come from 20% of inputs, so identify and double down on the vital few.
entries.description: An empirical heuristic noting that outputs are rarely distributed evenly across inputs. A small fraction of customers, code, or effort tends to drive the majority of revenue, bugs, or results. It is a power-law observation, not a precise law — the split could be 90/10 or 70/30, but the asymmetry is the point. Use it to find leverage rather than to grind on every task equally.
entries.example: A SaaS founder reviews her revenue and finds 3 of 50 customers generate 78% of monthly recurring revenue. She reallocates her support team to provide white-glove service to those three accounts and stops spending evening hours on long-tail trial users.
entries.howToApply: Once a quarter, list your tasks/clients/projects and rank them by output (revenue, learning, impact). Cross out the bottom half and ask: what would change if I stopped doing these? Then schedule one calendar block per week dedicated only to expanding the top 20%.
entries.pitfalls: The numbers are not literal — chasing an exact 80/20 split is misuse. Some domains (safety, security, parenting) require attention to the long tail; you cannot 80/20 a building inspection. It also tempts neglect of foundational work that compounds slowly.
entries.origin: Vilfredo Pareto observed Italian land-ownership distribution in 1906; Joseph M. Juran reframed it as the 'vital few and trivial many' management principle in 1941.

entries.name: Parkinson's Law
entries.oneLiner: Work expands to fill the time available for its completion.
entries.description: Parkinson's satirical observation about bureaucracies: tasks swell to consume whatever budget of time you give them. Give yourself a week for an email and you will agonize for a week; give yourself ten minutes and it gets sent. The mechanism is partly perfectionism, partly procrastination, partly the planning fallacy in reverse — slack invites waste.
entries.example: A consultant blocks two hours to write a client proposal he keeps postponing. He sets a 45-minute timer instead, drafts a passable version, sends it, and the client signs without revisions — the extra 75 minutes he would have spent polishing produced no measurable gain.
entries.howToApply: Set artificial deadlines that are 30–50% shorter than your gut estimate. Use a visible countdown timer for any task you have been avoiding. Before starting, write down what 'good enough to ship' looks like so you stop when you hit it, not when the clock runs out.
entries.pitfalls: Compressing time can degrade quality on genuinely complex creative or safety-critical work — a surgeon should not Parkinson her appendectomy. Also a self-imposed crunch culture leads to chronic stress; use it on individual tasks, not as a lifestyle.
entries.origin: C. Northcote Parkinson, satirical essay in The Economist, 19 November 1955; expanded in the book Parkinson's Law: The Pursuit of Progress (1958).

entries.name: Eisenhower Matrix (Urgent/Important)
entries.oneLiner: Sort tasks by urgency and importance to decide what to do, schedule, delegate, or delete.
entries.description: A 2x2 grid: Important + Urgent (do now), Important + Not Urgent (schedule), Not Important + Urgent (delegate), Not Important + Not Urgent (drop). The point is to stop confusing 'this is loud' with 'this matters' — most knowledge workers spend their day in Q3 (urgent-but-trivial) at the expense of Q2 (important-but-quiet) work that actually compounds.
entries.example: On Monday morning a PM lists: prep board deck (Q2), reply to a vendor's pricing email (Q3), draft Q4 strategy doc (Q2), respond to Slack pings about the office printer (Q4). She schedules the strategy doc for 9–11am, delegates the vendor reply to her ops lead, and mutes the printer thread.
entries.howToApply: Each morning, write your top 8–10 tasks and assign each a quadrant. Block calendar time only for Q1 and Q2. Create a 'delegate' Slack list for Q3. Delete or archive Q4 ruthlessly. Review weekly: if Q1 is always full, you are under-investing in Q2 prevention work.
entries.pitfalls: Most popularizations attribute the matrix directly to Eisenhower, but he only described the urgent/important distinction — the grid was popularized later. People also overestimate their ability to delegate; in solo contexts Q3 just becomes 'do it cheaply.'
entries.origin: Dwight D. Eisenhower, Address to the Second Assembly of the World Council of Churches, 19 August 1954 (he attributed the line to a 'former college president'); popularized as a matrix by Stephen Covey in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989).

entries.name: Pomodoro Technique
entries.oneLiner: Work in 25-minute focused intervals separated by short breaks, with a longer break every four cycles.
entries.description: A timer-based protocol that turns abstract 'work hard' intentions into concrete, finite sprints. The fixed length lowers the activation cost of starting and provides natural micro-deadlines that fight procrastination. Cirillo's rule 'if a Pomodoro begins, it has to ring' commits you to finishing one block before checking your phone — interruptions are noted on paper and handled in the break.
entries.example: A graduate student facing a dissertation chapter sets a kitchen timer for 25 minutes, writes without internet, stops mid-sentence when it dings, walks for 5 minutes, then runs three more pomodoros before lunch — producing 1,800 words on a day she would otherwise have spent reorganizing references.
entries.howToApply: Pick one task. Set a 25-minute timer (any tomato app, or a real timer). Close all tabs unrelated to the task. When the timer rings, take 5 minutes away from the screen. After four pomodoros, take 20–30 minutes off. Track completed pomodoros to estimate how big future tasks really are.
entries.pitfalls: 25 minutes is too short for some flow-state work (writing code, composing music) where ramp-up takes 15+ minutes; consider 50/10 splits. Rigid adherence can also fragment naturally long tasks. The technique helps with starting and pacing, not with choosing the right task in the first place.
entries.origin: Francesco Cirillo, developed in the late 1980s as a university student in Italy; formalized in his book The Pomodoro Technique (2006).

entries.name: Deep Work
entries.oneLiner: Focused, distraction-free work on cognitively demanding tasks is increasingly rare and increasingly valuable.
entries.description: Newport's thesis: high-skill knowledge work requires sustained, undistracted concentration that the modern attention economy actively undermines. He distinguishes 'deep work' (cognitively demanding, hard to replicate) from 'shallow work' (logistical, easily replaceable) and argues that depth is both a productivity multiplier and a meaning-generator. The economic claim: those who can produce at an elite level in fields requiring depth will disproportionately win in a connected economy.
entries.example: A software engineer schedules 9–12 every morning as a 'no Slack, no email, no meetings' block to design a new caching layer. Over six weeks she ships a system her always-online colleagues had been 'making progress on' for six months.
entries.howToApply: Block 60–120 minute chunks on your calendar labeled 'deep work,' phone in another room, single-tabbed browser. Pre-commit a clear goal for the block ('draft section 2 of the spec,' not 'work on spec'). Defend the block from meetings — if you must accept one, batch it with others. Track total deep hours per week; aim to grow it gradually toward 15–20.
entries.pitfalls: Some roles (manager, on-call SRE, ER nurse) are structurally shallow and cannot be re-engineered into long blocks. Deep-work absolutism can also become an excuse to ignore necessary collaboration and feedback. Newport's claim that social media harms careers is stronger as advice than as evidence.
entries.origin: Cal Newport, Deep Work: Rules for Focused Success in a Distracted World (Grand Central Publishing, 2016).

entries.name: Two-Minute Rule
entries.oneLiner: If a task takes less than two minutes, do it now instead of capturing it for later.
entries.description: From Allen's Getting Things Done. The reasoning is simple economics: the overhead of writing a task down, sorting it, scheduling it, and re-reading it later is greater than the two minutes the task itself costs. The rule is meant to be applied during inbox processing, not as a permission to be reactive all day — you only run it when you are already triaging.
entries.example: Processing email after lunch, a designer sees a request for the link to last week's Figma file. Instead of starring it for later, she pastes the link in 20 seconds and archives the thread. Twelve such micro-replies in 15 minutes empty her inbox.
entries.howToApply: Schedule two daily 'inbox processing' windows (e.g., 11:30 and 4:30). For each item, ask: actionable? If yes and under two minutes, do it immediately. If longer, defer to a project list or calendar. Keep a stopwatch handy at first — most 'two-minute' tasks turn out to be five.
entries.pitfalls: Misused as a justification for context-switching all day; the rule applies during dedicated triage, not during deep work. Many tasks people estimate as two minutes balloon into twenty. James Clear's habit-formation 'two-minute rule' is a different idea — do not conflate them.
entries.origin: David Allen, Getting Things Done: The Art of Stress-Free Productivity (Viking, 2001; revised edition 2015).

entries.name: Eat the Frog
entries.oneLiner: Do your hardest, most important task first thing in the morning, before anything else.
entries.description: Tracy borrows a line often misattributed to Mark Twain — 'eat a live frog first thing in the morning and nothing worse will happen the rest of the day' — and turns it into a single-sentence productivity rule. The 'frog' is the task with the largest impact you are most tempted to avoid. Doing it first exploits morning willpower and removes the dread that otherwise drains attention all day.
entries.example: A founder dreads writing the investor update. Instead of opening Slack at 9am, he opens a blank doc, writes the update in 40 minutes, sends it, and discovers the rest of his day is unusually focused — the background anxiety is gone.
entries.howToApply: The night before, write down tomorrow's single most consequential task. In the morning, do not check email, news, or messaging until that task is started. Treat the first 60–90 minutes as sacred. If you have two frogs, eat the uglier one first.
entries.pitfalls: Not everyone is a morning chronotype — for night owls forcing hard work at 7am can be counterproductive; the principle is really 'do the frog at your peak hours.' Also, the popular Twain quote attribution is unverified; the underlying advice is sound regardless.
entries.origin: Brian Tracy, Eat That Frog! 21 Great Ways to Stop Procrastinating and Get More Done in Less Time (Berrett-Koehler, 2001).

entries.name: Time Blocking
entries.oneLiner: Pre-assign every hour of your day to a specific task or category before the day starts.
entries.description: Rather than working from a to-do list and reacting to interruptions, you treat your calendar as the source of truth: each block names what you will do during it. The technique forces honest capacity planning — you cannot block 14 hours into an 8-hour day — and converts vague intentions into appointments with yourself. Variants include 'day theming' (Monday = writing, Tuesday = meetings) and 'task batching' (all email between 11 and 11:30).
entries.example: A product manager replaces her chaotic to-do list with a Google Calendar where 8–9 is 'roadmap doc,' 9–10 is 'standup + Slack,' 10–12 is 'customer interviews,' 1–2 is 'email batch,' 2–4 is 'spec review.' By Friday she has shipped the roadmap she had been carrying on the list for three weeks.
entries.howToApply: Each evening, drag tasks from your list onto tomorrow's calendar in 30–90 minute blocks. Color-code by category (deep work, admin, meetings, recovery). Leave 20–30% buffer for overruns and the unexpected. At day's end, compare actual vs. planned; over a few weeks your estimates calibrate.
entries.pitfalls: Reactive roles (support, sales, on-call) cannot block-plan tightly — buffer must dominate. Over-tight blocks create guilt when reality intervenes; aim for directional, not literal, adherence. Calendar maximalism can also become procrastination disguised as planning.
entries.origin: Practiced by Benjamin Franklin in his 1791 Autobiography (his hourly daily schedule); popularized in modern form by Cal Newport (Deep Work, 2016) and treated formally in his Time-Block Planner (2020).

entries.name: Single-Tasking (Anti-Multitasking)
entries.oneLiner: Doing one thing at a time produces more and better output than juggling several, because task-switching has real cognitive cost.
entries.description: Cognitive psychology has shown repeatedly that what feels like multitasking is rapid task-switching, and each switch incurs a 'switch cost' in time and accuracy. Heavy media multitaskers in Stanford studies performed worse on filtering, memory, and switching tasks than light multitaskers. Single-tasking is the deliberate practice of finishing — or at least pausing cleanly from — one task before starting another.
entries.example: An analyst building a financial model closes Slack, email, and his second monitor's news feed. The model that took two distracted days now takes four focused hours, and the formula errors he kept catching disappear.
entries.howToApply: Use one window, one tab, one document. Put the phone in a drawer or another room — proximity alone degrades attention (Ward et al., 2017). Batch communications into 2–3 windows per day. When interrupted, write down where you were before responding so re-entry is cheap.
entries.pitfalls: Some 'multitasking' is just background automation (walking while listening, cooking while on a podcast) and is fine. The Stanford finding (Ophir, Nass, Wagner, 2009) is correlational — heavy multitaskers may have been worse at filtering to begin with. Do not weaponize 'no interruptions' against teammates whose work depends on your input.
entries.origin: Foundational task-switching cost research: Rogers & Monsell, Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1995; media-multitasking study: Ophir, Nass & Wagner, PNAS, 2009. Popularized by writers including Daniel Goleman (Focus, 2013) and Cal Newport.

entries.name: Ivy Lee Method
entries.oneLiner: Each evening, write down the six most important things to do tomorrow in priority order, then work them sequentially.
entries.description: A century-old, deliberately minimal system. The constraints — six items, ranked, no skipping, write it the night before — are the whole technique. The cap on six forces real prioritization; the ranking removes morning decision fatigue; the sequential rule prevents the procrastination of cherry-picking the easy item first. Anything not finished simply rolls to tomorrow's list (after re-prioritization).
entries.example: A startup CEO writes her six tomorrow each night: 1) finalize term sheet, 2) review eng hiring loop, 3) call two unhappy customers, 4) board prep slide, 5) review Q3 burn, 6) reply to investor intros. She works them top-down and ends each day having done what mattered, even when she does not finish all six.
entries.howToApply: Tonight, on paper, write six tasks for tomorrow ranked 1–6 by importance. Tomorrow, start at #1 and do not move to #2 until #1 is done or genuinely blocked. At day's end, move incomplete items into a fresh ranked list for the next day. Do this for two weeks before judging.
entries.pitfalls: Not all work is a serial queue — managers and parents constantly handle interrupts. The famous '$25,000 advice' story is well-attested but specific dollar figures and quotes vary across retellings; treat it as illustrative, not gospel. Six can be too many for a heavy-meeting day; three is often more honest.
entries.origin: Ivy Ledbetter Lee, advising Charles M. Schwab of Bethlehem Steel, circa 1918; the story was widely circulated after Schwab reportedly paid Lee $25,000 (about $475,000 in 2025 dollars) for the method.

entries.name: Placebo Effect
entries.oneLiner: Inert treatments can produce real physiological and symptom relief when a person expects them to work.
entries.description: The placebo effect is a measurable improvement in a patient's condition triggered by belief in a treatment rather than its active pharmacology. Brain imaging shows real changes in pain pathways, dopamine release, and immune markers. It works strongest for subjective outcomes like pain, nausea, depression, fatigue, and Parkinsonian motor symptoms; it does not shrink tumors or cure infections.
entries.example: In open-label placebo trials by Ted Kaptchuk at Harvard, IBS and chronic-pain patients told 'these are sugar pills with no drug' still reported significant symptom relief versus no-treatment controls.
entries.howToApply: Build small expectancy rituals around things you actually want to work: take vitamins at the same time daily, use a 'focus playlist' before deep work, do a pre-workout routine. When evaluating a new supplement or therapy, demand randomized placebo-controlled evidence before trusting personal anecdotes.
entries.pitfalls: Placebo response is often confused with the natural course of illness or regression to the mean. It does not justify homeopathy, reiki, or unproven cancer treatments. Effect sizes shrink dramatically in well-blinded trials with objective endpoints.
entries.origin: Term popularized by Henry K. Beecher's 1955 paper 'The Powerful Placebo' in JAMA; concept described in medical literature since the 18th century.

entries.name: Nocebo Effect
entries.oneLiner: Negative expectations alone can produce real adverse symptoms, even from inert treatments.
entries.description: The nocebo effect is the placebo's evil twin: when patients expect harm, side effects, or pain, they often experience them. Reviews in JAMA and The Lancet show that informed-consent warnings, news coverage of drug side effects, and statin discontinuation studies all produce real symptoms in patients taking sugar pills.
entries.example: In the SAMSON trial (NEJM, 2020), patients who had stopped statins citing side effects reported 90% of the same symptoms when taking placebo capsules, demonstrating most reported statin side effects were nocebo-driven.
entries.howToApply: Be careful what symptom lists you read before taking medication; ask your doctor for the base rate of side effects rather than the full warning sheet. Reframe physical sensations neutrally ('my heart is beating faster' vs 'I'm having a panic attack'). Avoid doom-scrolling symptoms when sick.
entries.pitfalls: Do not weaponize this to dismiss patients reporting real adverse effects; many drug side effects are pharmacological and serious. The line between nocebo and genuine reaction requires blinded testing, not gaslighting.
entries.origin: Term coined by Walter Kennedy in 1961; mechanism formalized in pain research by Fabrizio Benedetti starting in the 1990s.

entries.name: Hawthorne Effect
entries.oneLiner: People modify their behavior when they know they are being observed or measured.
entries.description: Named for the Hawthorne Works factory studies (1924-1932), the effect describes short-term performance boosts produced by attention itself rather than the intervention being tested. Modern reanalyses by Levitt and List (2011) found the original lighting-experiment data was weaker than legend, but the broader phenomenon, observation changes behavior, is robustly demonstrated in healthcare hand-hygiene and workplace studies.
entries.example: Hospital hand-hygiene compliance commonly jumps from ~30% to over 70% when staff know auditors are watching the ward, and falls back when audits end. Fitbit users walk more in the first weeks of wearing the device, then drift back.
entries.howToApply: Engineer benign observation into habits you want to keep: workout buddies, public commitment, shared sleep trackers, body-doubling co-working sessions. When measuring whether a change worked, control for the boost from being watched by running a longer follow-up or a control group.
entries.pitfalls: The original 'lighting study' narrative is partly mythologized; effect sizes in field settings are smaller and often fade. Confusing 'the team got better because we measured it' with real process improvement leads to bad management decisions.
entries.origin: Coined by Henry A. Landsberger in 1958 reanalyzing Elton Mayo's Hawthorne Works productivity studies of the 1920s-30s.

entries.name: Pygmalion Effect
entries.oneLiner: Higher expectations from teachers or leaders cause better performance in students or subordinates.
entries.description: Rosenthal and Jacobson's 'Pygmalion in the Classroom' (1968) showed that when teachers were told certain randomly-chosen students were 'late bloomers,' those students gained more IQ points by year-end. Subsequent meta-analyses (Raudenbush 1984, Jussim & Harber 2005) found the effect is real but modest, strongest with younger children and new teachers, and smaller than the original study suggested.
entries.example: An IDF study by Eden (1990) showed platoons whose commanders were told their soldiers had 'high command potential' scored significantly higher on objective tests than control platoons, despite identical actual ability distributions.
entries.howToApply: When managing or teaching, write down your honest expectations for each person and notice if you are subtly under-coaching anyone. Give specific challenge tasks ('I'm giving this to you because I think you can handle it') rather than generic praise. Audit which direct reports get the hardest assignments.
entries.pitfalls: The original Rosenthal-Jacobson IQ-gain effect has been hard to replicate at full strength. Do not expect mere positive thinking to overcome structural barriers, lack of skill, or insufficient resources. Inflated expectations without support produce burnout, not growth.
entries.origin: Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson, 'Pygmalion in the Classroom' (1968); name from George Bernard Shaw's play.

entries.name: Zeigarnik Effect
entries.oneLiner: Unfinished tasks occupy mental bandwidth more than completed ones, intruding on attention until closed.
entries.description: Bluma Zeigarnik's 1927 dissertation found waiters could recall unpaid orders better than paid ones, and lab subjects remembered interrupted tasks roughly twice as well as completed tasks. Later replications (notably Masicampo & Baumeister 2011) show that simply making a concrete plan to finish a task can release the cognitive grip even before completion.
entries.example: Cliffhanger episode endings on Netflix drive auto-play because the unresolved plot keeps your attention engaged. Open browser tabs you 'will read later' silently consume working memory until you either read, save, or close them.
entries.howToApply: When a task intrudes at night, write down a specific next step and time ('Tuesday 9am: email Sam draft v2'); studies show this defuses rumination as effectively as finishing it. Close loops daily: declare end-of-day, capture open items in one trusted list, then disengage.
entries.pitfalls: Replication of Zeigarnik's original recall ratio has been mixed; the strong 2:1 effect is unreliable, but the rumination-from-open-loops mechanism holds up well. Do not use it as an excuse to leave everything half-done as a 'motivation hack'.
entries.origin: Bluma Zeigarnik, working under Kurt Lewin in Berlin, 1927 dissertation.

entries.name: IKEA Effect
entries.oneLiner: People overvalue things they partially built themselves, regardless of objective quality.
entries.description: Norton, Mochon, and Ariely (2012) showed subjects who assembled IKEA boxes, folded origami, or built Lego sets bid significantly more for their own creations than equivalent items made by others, and rated their amateur work close to expert work. The effect requires successful completion and genuine effort, not just any labor.
entries.example: Founders routinely overvalue their own startups and resist pivots. Home cooks rate their own meals higher than diners do. Crypto holders defend tokens whose whitepapers they read carefully even after fundamentals deteriorate.
entries.howToApply: Before big decisions about something you built, get a third party with no skin in the game to price it or critique it. When selling something you made, anchor on comparable market sales, not on hours spent. Conversely, exploit it ethically: customers who help configure your product retain better.
entries.pitfalls: Overlaps with sunk-cost fallacy and endowment effect; do not let pride in construction lock you into a losing project. The effect collapses if the build fails, so half-built projects can flip to aversion.
entries.origin: Michael I. Norton, Daniel Mochon, and Dan Ariely, Journal of Consumer Psychology, 2012.

entries.name: Endowment Effect
entries.oneLiner: People demand more to give up something they own than they would pay to acquire it.
entries.description: Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler's 1990 mug experiments showed that subjects randomly given a coffee mug demanded roughly twice the price to sell it as buyers would pay, despite identical objective value. The effect is grounded in loss aversion: losses loom about twice as large as equivalent gains.
entries.example: Homeowners price their homes above market and refuse offers near appraisal. Employees turn down better job offers because changing means giving up familiar perks. Investors hold losing stocks too long because selling 'realizes' the loss.
entries.howToApply: Run the 'reversal test': if you didn't already own this stock, house, job, or relationship, would you buy in at today's price and terms? If no, that is your answer. For negotiations, frame concessions as gains for the counterparty rather than losses.
entries.pitfalls: Recent work (Plott & Zeiler 2005, 2007) shows much of the effect disappears with proper experimental procedures and experienced traders, suggesting some 'endowment' is misunderstanding of the task. The effect is real but weaker for fungible goods (cash, commodities) and for traders with market experience.
entries.origin: Term coined by Richard Thaler in 1980; canonical demonstration by Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler in Journal of Political Economy, 1990.

entries.name: Spotlight Effect
entries.oneLiner: We dramatically overestimate how much other people notice and remember our appearance, mistakes, and quirks.
entries.description: Gilovich, Medvec, and Savitsky (2000) had Cornell students wear an embarrassing Barry Manilow T-shirt into a room of peers; wearers estimated about 50% would notice, but only ~25% actually did, and even fewer remembered later. The bias stems from egocentric anchoring: we cannot easily simulate others' attention, which is mostly on themselves.
entries.example: Stumbling over a word in a presentation feels devastating; almost no one in the audience remembers it the next day. A bad haircut feels universally noticed; coworkers usually don't comment because they barely registered it.
entries.howToApply: Before social anxiety derails action, ask: 'Will anyone here remember this in 48 hours?' If no, proceed. Use this to lower the cost of asking dumb questions, public speaking, dating, networking, and looking foolish while learning a new skill.
entries.pitfalls: Do not over-apply this in genuinely high-stakes professional or reputational contexts where people are evaluating you on purpose (interviews, performance reviews, public-facing roles). The effect is about incidental observation, not deliberate evaluation.
entries.origin: Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec, and Kenneth Savitsky, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2000.

entries.name: Bystander Effect
entries.oneLiner: The more witnesses to an emergency, the less likely any single person is to intervene.
entries.description: Darley and Latané's 1968 experiments, prompted by the Kitty Genovese murder coverage, found that subjects intervened ~85% of the time when alone with a victim but only ~31% when in a group of five, due to diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance. Recent CCTV-based meta-analysis (Philpot et al. 2020) found that in real public-place emergencies, intervention by at least one bystander actually occurs over 90% of the time, complicating the classic story.
entries.example: In a crowded subway, a passenger collapses and dozens hesitate, each assuming someone else has called help. In a Slack channel of 200, an obvious bug report sits unanswered for hours; in a DM the same question gets answered in two minutes.
entries.howToApply: If you need help, name a specific person ('You in the blue jacket, call 911'); this collapses diffusion. If you witness something wrong, act first or speak first to break pluralistic ignorance, others usually follow. In email and Slack, address one named owner, never 'the team'.
entries.pitfalls: The Kitty Genovese 38-witnesses story was largely inaccurate (NY Times retracted parts). Real-world intervention rates are much higher than lab studies imply, especially when the situation is unambiguous. Do not assume crowds will always freeze; assume crowds will follow whoever moves first.
entries.origin: John Darley and Bibb Latané, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1968.

entries.name: Self-Fulfilling Prophecy
entries.oneLiner: A belief about a future outcome causes behavior that makes that outcome more likely to occur.
entries.description: Robert K. Merton formalized the concept in 1948: a false definition of a situation evokes new behavior that makes the originally false conception come true. It operates at individual scale (expecting rejection, you act distant, are then rejected) and systemic scale (a rumored bank insolvency triggers withdrawals that cause insolvency). It is the general mechanism underneath the Pygmalion effect and stereotype threat.
entries.example: Believing 'I'm bad at math' leads to less practice and avoidance of challenging problems, producing the predicted poor performance. The 2008 run on Northern Rock was triggered when fear of insolvency caused the deposit run that actually caused insolvency.
entries.howToApply: Audit your prophecies: write the belief, then list the behaviors it produces, then ask whether those behaviors cause the outcome. To break a negative one, change the behavior first ('act as if'); to install a positive one, set up environment cues that make the desired behavior automatic.
entries.pitfalls: Not all expectations are self-fulfilling; many beliefs simply track reality. Overusing this concept slides into magical thinking ('manifesting'). Stereotype-threat literature, a key application, has had mixed replication, so claims should rest on the specific study, not the general meme.
entries.origin: Robert K. Merton, 'The Self-Fulfilling Prophecy,' Antioch Review, 1948; concept rooted in W.I. Thomas's 1928 'Thomas theorem'.

entries.name: Gottman's Four Horsemen
entries.oneLiner: Four destructive communication patterns—criticism, contempt, defensiveness, and stonewalling—that strongly predict relationship breakdown.
entries.description: John Gottman identified four communication behaviors that consistently predict divorce in longitudinal lab studies of couples. Criticism attacks character; contempt expresses moral superiority via mockery, sarcasm, or eye-rolling; defensiveness deflects responsibility; stonewalling shuts down under physiological flooding. Contempt is the single strongest predictor. Each has an antidote: gentle start-up, building admiration, taking responsibility, and self-soothing.
entries.example: Instead of 'You never help around here, you're so lazy' (criticism + contempt), try 'I felt overwhelmed when the dishes piled up. Could we split them tonight?' (gentle start-up + clear request).
entries.howToApply: 1) Catch yourself before sentences starting with 'You always/never.' 2) Replace 'You' attacks with 'I felt X when Y happened. I need Z.' 3) When flooded (heart rate >100), call a 20-minute timeout and self-soothe before continuing. 4) Track contempt specifically—zero-tolerance rule. 5) When criticized, find the 1% you can own.
entries.pitfalls: The 90%+ divorce-prediction accuracy was on a specific sample and post-hoc; prospective predictive accuracy is lower. Don't weaponize the framework to label your partner mid-fight ('that's contempt!')—that itself is contempt. Stonewalling can be a trauma response, not malice.
entries.origin: John Gottman & Robert Levenson, longitudinal couples research from the 1970s onward; popularized in 'Why Marriages Succeed or Fail' (1994).

entries.name: 5:1 Positivity Ratio (Magic Ratio)
entries.oneLiner: Stable couples maintain at least five positive interactions for every negative one during conflict.
entries.description: Drawn from Gottman and Levenson's observational research, stable, satisfied marriages averaged about 5:1 positive-to-negative interactions during conflict, while couples heading for divorce averaged closer to 0.8:1. Positive interactions include interest, affection, humor, validation, apology, and small acts of repair. The ratio is during conflict; outside conflict the ratio is closer to 20:1 in happy couples.
entries.example: After a tense disagreement about money, you tease your partner gently, touch their arm, agree on one thing they said, thank them for raising it, and apologize for your tone—five small positives offsetting one sharp comment.
entries.howToApply: 1) During an argument, deliberately insert humor, agreement, or affection. 2) End every disagreement with one explicit appreciation. 3) Keep daily 'small things often': 6-second kisses, 20-minute stress-reducing conversations. 4) Audit your last fight—count positives vs negatives honestly.
entries.pitfalls: The unrelated Losada/Fredrickson '3:1 positivity ratio' for individuals was mathematically debunked (Brown, Sokal & Friedman, 2013); don't conflate them. Gottman's 5:1 holds up better but is descriptive, not a precise prescription—forced positivity feels fake. Faking warmth around abuse or neglect is harmful.
entries.origin: John Gottman & Robert Levenson, University of Washington 'Love Lab,' published findings 1992–1999.

entries.name: Active Listening
entries.oneLiner: Listening with full attention and reflecting back meaning so the speaker feels accurately understood.
entries.description: Coined by Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957, active listening is the disciplined practice of attending to a speaker's content, feeling, and meaning, then paraphrasing or reflecting to confirm understanding before responding. Core moves include eye contact, open questions, reflecting feelings, summarizing, and suspending judgment and advice. It builds trust and reduces misunderstanding in counseling, medicine, negotiation, and intimate relationships.
entries.example: Partner: 'I'm exhausted, work is brutal.' Reactive reply: 'You should quit.' Active listening: 'Sounds like you're running on fumes and don't see relief coming. What's been the worst part this week?'
entries.howToApply: 1) Put the phone face-down, body squared toward speaker. 2) Before replying, paraphrase: 'So what I'm hearing is…' 3) Name the feeling you sense: 'That sounds frustrating.' 4) Ask one open question before offering advice. 5) Resist the urge to fix; ask 'Do you want support or solutions?'
entries.pitfalls: Mechanical paraphrasing ('I hear you saying…') feels robotic and patronizing. Active listening alone doesn't fix incompatible needs or abuse. Effects on outcomes are context-dependent and modest in some studies. Don't use it as a debate tactic to seem fair while ignoring the substance.
entries.origin: Carl Rogers & Richard Farson, 1957 paper 'Active Listening,' University of Chicago Industrial Relations Center.

entries.name: Five Love Languages
entries.oneLiner: Chapman's claim that people give and receive love primarily through one of five modes—words, time, gifts, service, or touch.
entries.description: Gary Chapman's 1992 book proposes that mismatched 'love languages' explain why partners feel unloved despite effort. The five are: words of affirmation, quality time, receiving gifts, acts of service, and physical touch. Identifying and 'speaking' your partner's primary language is meant to increase felt love. The framework is widely used in couples coaching but rests on weaker empirical evidence than its popularity suggests.
entries.example: Your partner cooks elaborate meals (acts of service) but craves verbal praise (words of affirmation). Both feel unappreciated until each starts giving in the other's preferred mode—daily 'thank you, that meant a lot' alongside the cooking.
entries.howToApply: 1) Each partner ranks the five from most to least meaningful when receiving. 2) Share lists; do not assume your top is theirs. 3) Once a week, deliver one deliberate act in your partner's top language. 4) Use it as a conversation starter, not a personality test.
entries.pitfalls: A 2022–2023 review (Impett, Park & Muise) concluded the love-languages model lacks empirical support: people don't reliably have one stable primary language, matching couples don't show higher satisfaction, and the 5-category structure isn't well-validated. Treat it as a useful conversation prompt, not a typology. Risk: using it to demand love only on your terms or to excuse not learning the others.
entries.origin: Gary Chapman, 'The Five Love Languages,' Northfield Publishing, 1992.

entries.name: Bids for Connection
entries.oneLiner: Small attempts—a comment, glance, or touch—to get a partner's attention, affection, or support.
entries.description: Gottman calls bids 'the fundamental unit of emotional communication.' A bid can be verbal ('Look at that bird') or nonverbal (a sigh, a hand on the shoulder). Partners 'turn toward' (engage), 'turn away' (ignore), or 'turn against' (snap). In Gottman's lab, couples who stayed married six years later turned toward bids about 86% of the time; those who divorced did so only 33% of the time.
entries.example: Your partner says 'Huh, weird headline' while scrolling. Turning toward: 'Oh? What does it say?' Turning away: silence. Turning against: 'Can you not narrate every article?' The first builds; the others erode.
entries.howToApply: 1) Treat any conversational opener as a bid—answer it, even briefly. 2) Lift your eyes from screens within 3 seconds when your partner speaks. 3) Make small bids yourself daily: share an observation, ask a tiny question. 4) If you can't engage, defer warmly: 'Tell me in 10 minutes—I want to hear it.'
entries.pitfalls: The 86% / 33% figures come from a small, specific sample and have not been broadly independently replicated. Constant turning toward at the cost of focus or boundaries is also unhealthy. Bids can be passive-aggressive; not every 'turning away' is rejection—context matters.
entries.origin: John Gottman, 'The Relationship Cure' (2001) and Love Lab research from the 1990s.

entries.name: Repair Attempts
entries.oneLiner: Any statement or action that prevents negativity from escalating during conflict.
entries.description: Gottman's research shows that what distinguishes lasting couples isn't avoiding fights but successfully repairing them mid-argument. A repair attempt can be a joke, a softening, an apology, taking responsibility, or asking for a break. The key finding: in stable couples, repair attempts succeed because partners have a strong underlying friendship; in distressed couples, even good repairs are rejected.
entries.example: Mid-argument, one partner says 'Wait—I'm being a jerk. Can we start over?' or makes a private inside-joke face. The other softens, laughs, and the spiral breaks.
entries.howToApply: 1) Pre-agree on a repair phrase ('let's reset' or a silly word) you can use without losing face. 2) Use physiological cues—racing heart, clenched jaw—as a signal to repair. 3) Repairs in early seconds work best; the longer you wait, the harder. 4) Accept your partner's clumsy repairs—rejecting them trains them to stop trying.
entries.pitfalls: Repair without addressing the underlying issue becomes avoidance. Humor as repair can land as mockery if timed badly. In abusive dynamics, 'repair' from the harmer can manipulate the harmed into dropping legitimate concerns. Don't expect a single repair to substitute for accountability.
entries.origin: John Gottman, formalized in 'The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work' (1999).

entries.name: Empathy vs Sympathy
entries.oneLiner: Empathy feels with someone; sympathy feels for them—and only empathy creates genuine connection.
entries.description: Brené Brown, drawing on nurse-researcher Theresa Wiseman's 1996 framework, distinguishes empathy from sympathy: sympathy looks down at suffering ('that's too bad') and often deflects with silver linings ('at least…'); empathy climbs into the dark with the person. Wiseman's four attributes of empathy are: perspective-taking, staying out of judgment, recognizing emotion in others, and communicating that recognition. Empathy rarely starts with 'at least.'
entries.example: Friend: 'I had a miscarriage.' Sympathy: 'At least you can try again.' Empathy: 'I don't know what to say. I'm so glad you told me—this is heavy.'
entries.howToApply: 1) Replace 'at least' with 'that sounds…' followed by the feeling. 2) Resist the urge to fix, compare, or silver-line in the first response. 3) Name what you imagine they feel and check: 'That sounds terrifying—am I close?' 4) Sit in silence longer than feels comfortable. 5) Share vulnerability rather than advice.
entries.pitfalls: Empathy without limits leads to emotional fusion and burnout—therapists distinguish 'cognitive empathy' from 'emotional contagion.' Performing empathy ('I totally get it') without genuine perspective-taking feels worse than honest sympathy. Don't claim to know exactly how someone feels if you don't.
entries.origin: Theresa Wiseman, 'A concept analysis of empathy,' Journal of Advanced Nursing, 1996; popularized by Brené Brown in 'Daring Greatly' (2012) and the 2013 RSA short animation.

entries.name: Healthy Boundaries
entries.oneLiner: Clear personal rules about what you will and won't accept, expressed without controlling others.
entries.description: A boundary is a self-governing rule about your own behavior in response to others—'where my feelings end and yours begin.' Healthy boundaries are flexible (not rigid walls, not porous), conscious, and stated clearly. They can be physical, emotional, time-based, financial, or digital. The point isn't to change another person but to define what you will do if a line is crossed.
entries.example: 'I won't continue conversations where I'm being yelled at. If voices rise, I'll step away for an hour and we can try again.' That's a boundary. 'You can't yell at me' is a demand.
entries.howToApply: 1) Phrase boundaries as your action, not their behavior: 'I will leave the room if…' 2) State once, calmly, in neutral times—not mid-fight. 3) Follow through every time; an unenforced boundary is a wish. 4) Distinguish negotiable preferences from non-negotiables (safety, dignity, fidelity). 5) Audit your boundaries yearly—rigid rules from past hurt may need updating.
entries.pitfalls: 'Boundaries' has become pop-psychology shorthand for one-sided ultimatums or refusal to be accountable. Real boundaries govern your behavior, not your partner's. They aren't punishments or stonewalling. Cross-cultural research questions universal applicability—collectivist contexts may frame interdependence differently. Setting boundaries with abusers can escalate danger; safety planning may matter more than communication.
entries.origin: Concept formalized in Anne Katherine's 'Boundaries: Where You End and I Begin' (1991) and Cloud & Townsend's 'Boundaries' (1992); Nina Brown's typology (soft/spongy/rigid/flexible) elaborated it.

entries.name: Nonviolent Communication (NVC)
entries.oneLiner: A four-step framework for honest expression and empathic listening: observation, feeling, need, request.
entries.description: Marshall Rosenberg developed NVC during civil-rights-era mediation work. The model separates observable facts from interpretations, names the feeling triggered, links it to a universal human need (safety, respect, rest), and ends with a clear, doable, refusable request. The same four steps work in reverse for empathic listening—guessing the other's observation, feeling, need, and request beneath their words.
entries.example: Instead of 'You're so disrespectful, you ignored me all night,' try: 'When you looked at your phone during dinner (observation), I felt lonely (feeling) because I need connection after a long day (need). Would you put it on the shelf during meals this week? (request)'
entries.howToApply: 1) Drill the formula in writing first—it feels stilted aloud until practiced. 2) Strip evaluation from observation: replace 'you were rude' with the specific behavior. 3) Use a feelings-and-needs list (Rosenberg's CNVC publishes one) to expand vocabulary beyond 'fine/upset.' 4) Make requests doable in 24 hours, not vague ('be more loving'). 5) Accept 'no'—a request that can't be refused is a demand.
entries.pitfalls: Evidence base is thin: studies are small, heterogeneous, and often by NVC-affiliated authors. Mechanically applied, NVC can sound performative or manipulative ('I'm hearing you say…'). It can be misused to shame partners for 'doing it wrong' or to avoid accountability by reframing harm as unmet needs. Power imbalances and abuse aren't solved by better grammar. Some collectivist cultures find explicit feeling-disclosure intrusive.
entries.origin: Marshall Rosenberg, formalized in training manuals from 1972 and the book 'Nonviolent Communication: A Language of Life' (1999, 2003).

entries.name: Emotional Bank Account
entries.oneLiner: Trust in a relationship behaves like a bank balance: small deposits compound, withdrawals cost more than they seem.
entries.description: Stephen Covey's metaphor in Habit 5 of 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People.' Every interaction is a deposit (kept promises, kindness, listening, apologies, integrity) or a withdrawal (broken promises, criticism, dishonesty, taking for granted). A high balance lets the relationship absorb mistakes and hard conversations; a low balance means even small slights overdraw the account. Covey lists six major deposits, including understanding the individual, attending to little things, keeping commitments, clarifying expectations, showing personal integrity, and apologizing sincerely.
entries.example: You've been late to dinners three weeks running (withdrawals). When you finally raise a sensitive concern about money, your partner reacts sharply—not because the concern is unfair but because the account is overdrawn.
entries.howToApply: 1) Make one deliberate deposit daily: a thank-you, a kept micro-promise, a remembered detail. 2) Before a hard conversation, check the balance—if low, deposit first. 3) When you withdraw, apologize specifically and quickly—delayed apologies depreciate. 4) Track patterns: which behaviors does your partner experience as deposits vs withdrawals? They're not always what you'd predict.
entries.pitfalls: It's a metaphor, not a transaction—'I did three nice things, you owe me' is keeping score, which itself is a withdrawal. Deposits in your currency may not register in theirs (links to love-languages caveat). The model can let chronic harmers paper over real damage with small kindnesses; some withdrawals (betrayal, abuse) can't be offset by deposits.
entries.origin: Stephen R. Covey, 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People,' Free Press, 1989.
