entries.name: Reciprocity Principle
entries.oneLiner: People feel obligated to repay favors, gifts, and concessions, even unsolicited ones from strangers.
entries.description: Reciprocity is a near-universal social rule: when someone gives us something, we feel pressure to give back. Robert Cialdini documented how this drives compliance in sales, fundraising, and politics. The obligation is triggered even by trivial or unwanted favors, and the return gift is often disproportionately larger.
entries.example: A waiter who leaves a small mint with the bill increases tips by roughly 3 percent; leaving two mints and a personal comment increases tips by around 23 percent (Strohmetz et al., 2002, Journal of Applied Social Psychology). Free samples at Costco function the same way.
entries.howToApply: Give first, specifically and unexpectedly, before you need anything. When someone tries to use this on you (free pen with a donation envelope, an unsolicited gift from a vendor), name it internally and decline the implicit debt without guilt. In negotiations, make a real concession to trigger one back.
entries.pitfalls: Reciprocity is exploited by cults, timeshare pitches, and manipulative gift-giving. It can also breed resentment if recipients feel cornered. Gifts that look strategic backfire; sincerity matters. Effect sizes vary across cultures (collectivist vs. individualist).
entries.origin: Robert Cialdini, Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion (1984); roots in Marcel Mauss, The Gift (1925) and Alvin Gouldner's 'norm of reciprocity' (1960).

entries.name: Social Proof
entries.oneLiner: When uncertain, people copy what similar others are doing and treat popularity as evidence of correctness.
entries.description: Social proof is the heuristic that 'if many people are doing it, it must be right.' It is strongest under ambiguity and when the model group is similar to us. Cialdini lists it as one of six core influence principles; it underlies herd behavior, viral trends, and bystander effects.
entries.example: Asch's line-judgment conformity studies (1951, 1956) showed about 75 percent of subjects conformed to a clearly wrong majority at least once. Modern version: hotel towel-reuse signs that cite 'most guests in this room reused their towels' beat generic environmental appeals (Goldstein, Cialdini, Griskevicius, 2008, Journal of Consumer Research).
entries.howToApply: Use it to build healthy habits: join groups where the desired behavior is the default (running clubs, study cohorts). When evaluating a product, ask whether the 'crowd' is genuinely informed or just loud. For your own influence, show specific, similar peers doing the thing rather than abstract big numbers.
entries.pitfalls: Bandwagons can be manufactured (astroturfing, fake reviews, bot followers). Social proof from dissimilar crowds misleads. It also propagates panics and bubbles, where everyone is using everyone else as evidence with no underlying signal.
entries.origin: Solomon Asch's conformity experiments (1951); concept popularized as 'social proof' by Robert Cialdini (1984).

entries.name: Halo Effect
entries.oneLiner: One positive trait, especially attractiveness, contaminates judgment of unrelated traits like intelligence or honesty.
entries.description: The halo effect is a cognitive bias where overall impression of a person, brand, or thing colors evaluation of specific attributes. Edward Thorndike named it in 1920 after observing officers rated soldiers high on every trait once they liked them overall. It also runs in reverse (the 'horns effect').
entries.example: Attractive defendants receive lighter sentences in mock-jury studies (Stewart, 1980). Apple's iPod halo lifted Mac sales in the mid-2000s. In hiring, a candidate from a prestigious school is rated higher on coding ability before any code is seen.
entries.howToApply: Decouple judgments: when evaluating a hire, score each dimension independently before seeing the overall package, ideally blind. Use structured interviews and rubrics. When you catch yourself liking someone instantly, ask 'what specifically have they shown me about competence X?'
entries.pitfalls: Hard to debias by willpower alone, since it operates pre-consciously. 'Just be aware of it' has weak evidence; structural fixes (blind review, separated ratings) work better. Also confused with simple correlation: attractive people may genuinely have advantages from a lifetime of better treatment.
entries.origin: Edward Thorndike, 'A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings,' Journal of Applied Psychology (1920).

entries.name: Pratfall Effect
entries.oneLiner: Competent people become more likable after a small blunder; mediocre people become less likable.
entries.description: Elliot Aronson showed in 1966 that high-performing individuals who spilled coffee on themselves were rated more attractive than those who did not, while average performers were rated less attractive after the same gaffe. Visible imperfection humanizes the otherwise intimidating, but only if baseline competence is established.
entries.example: A senior engineer admitting 'I don't know, let me check' in a meeting tends to gain trust. Jennifer Lawrence tripping at the 2013 Oscars boosted her likability ratings. A struggling junior making the same admission may instead trigger doubt.
entries.howToApply: Once you have demonstrated competence, share a small, real flaw or mistake — it lowers defenses and signals honesty. In presentations, acknowledge the limitation of your data before opponents do. Do not manufacture pratfalls; they read as fake and trigger the opposite effect.
entries.pitfalls: Replication is mixed; effect sizes are modest and moderated by gender, status, and observer self-esteem. Strategic self-deprecation can look like impostor performance. The original 1966 study had a small sample (n=48) and has not been robustly meta-analyzed.
entries.origin: Elliot Aronson, Ben Willerman, and Joanne Floyd, Psychonomic Science (1966).

entries.name: Ben Franklin Effect
entries.oneLiner: Asking someone for a small favor makes them like you more, because they justify helping by deciding you were worth it.
entries.description: Counter-intuitive consequence of cognitive dissonance: when a person does you a favor, their brain reconciles the act by inferring positive feelings toward you. Franklin used it to win over a political rival by asking to borrow a rare book. Jecker and Landy formalized it experimentally in 1969.
entries.example: Jecker and Landy (1969) had subjects win money in a contest. When the experimenter later asked them to return it as a personal favor, those subjects rated him more favorably than subjects who were not asked. In modern life: asking a senior colleague for advice often warms the relationship faster than offering them help.
entries.howToApply: When you want to build rapport with someone unfamiliar or skeptical, ask for a small, specific, easy favor (an introduction, a five-minute opinion on a draft) — then thank them sincerely. Avoid stacking requests; one ask, well-placed, beats a series.
entries.pitfalls: Large or burdensome requests trigger the opposite (resentment). The effect competes with reciprocity, which says the giver should be liked more, not the receiver — context determines which dominates. Replication is moderate, not large.
entries.origin: Benjamin Franklin's autobiography (c. 1791); experimentally tested by Jon Jecker and David Landy, Human Relations (1969).

entries.name: Mere Exposure Effect
entries.oneLiner: Repeated exposure to something, even subliminal, tends to increase liking for it without any other reason.
entries.description: Robert Zajonc demonstrated in 1968 that simply seeing a stimulus more often (nonsense words, Chinese characters, faces) made people rate it more positively. The effect operates without conscious recognition and is one of the most robustly replicated findings in social psychology, with a meta-analytic effect size around r = 0.26 (Bornstein, 1989).
entries.example: You like a song more after the third radio play. Logos that seemed ugly become acceptable after a rebrand period. Classmates who sit nearer to you become friends more often than equally compatible classmates across the room (Festinger, Schachter, Back, 1950).
entries.howToApply: To build a relationship, increase low-pressure incidental contact (shared lunches, recurring meetings) before pitching anything. For products, prioritize sustained low-key visibility over one big launch. Personally, audit which preferences are real and which are 'I just keep seeing this.'
entries.pitfalls: Overexposure causes satiation and reversal. Negative initial reaction can be amplified, not softened, by repetition (e.g., divisive ads). The effect is weaker when the stimulus is consciously evaluated than when it is briefly or subliminally shown.
entries.origin: Robert Zajonc, 'Attitudinal Effects of Mere Exposure,' Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1968).

entries.name: Mirroring and Behavioral Mimicry
entries.oneLiner: Subtly matching another person's posture, speech, and gestures increases liking, trust, and cooperation.
entries.description: Chartrand and Bargh's 'chameleon effect' (1999) showed people unconsciously mimic interaction partners and that experimental confederates who mirrored subjects were rated more likable. Mimicry signals affiliation and seems to recruit shared neural representations, possibly via mirror systems.
entries.example: Van Baaren et al. (2003, 2004) found waitresses who repeated orders verbatim received about 70 percent larger tips than those who paraphrased. Successful negotiators tend to match counterparts' speech rate and energy level.
entries.howToApply: In conversation, match speaking pace and energy first, then posture; lag by a few seconds so it is not parroting. Repeat back the other person's exact key word once before paraphrasing. Drop it the moment it feels performative.
entries.pitfalls: Conscious, mechanical mimicry is detected and reads as creepy or manipulative. Cross-cultural norms for eye contact, touch, and proxemics vary widely. The 'mirror neuron' framing is contested; effects on liking are real, but the neuroscience story is oversold.
entries.origin: Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh, 'The Chameleon Effect,' Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1999).

entries.name: Dunbar's Number
entries.oneLiner: Humans can maintain stable social relationships with roughly 150 people, with tighter inner circles of 5, 15, and 50.
entries.description: Robin Dunbar (1992) correlated primate neocortex size with group size and extrapolated a human cognitive limit near 150. He later proposed nested layers: 5 close confidants, 15 good friends, 50 friends, 150 meaningful contacts, 500 acquaintances, 1,500 recognizable faces.
entries.example: Hutterite farming communities historically split when they pass roughly 150 members. Gore-Tex factories famously cap office size near 150. Your phone contacts may have thousands, but the people you would invite to a wedding rarely exceed this range.
entries.howToApply: Audit your inner 5 and 15: are they getting deliberate time? Treat 150 as a soft attention budget, not a target. When a community grows past it, expect coordination overhead and consider sub-groups before culture frays.
entries.pitfalls: The 150 figure has weak empirical grounding: a 2021 Stockholm University study (Lindenfors, Wartel, Lind) using updated primate data and modern statistics produced a 95 percent confidence interval ranging from about 4 to 520, and concluded the specific number is not justifiable. Treat it as a metaphor about cognitive limits, not a precise constant.
entries.origin: Robin Dunbar, 'Neocortex size as a constraint on group size in primates,' Journal of Human Evolution (1992).

entries.name: In-Group Bias (Minimal Group Paradigm)
entries.oneLiner: Even arbitrary group labels make people favor their own side and discriminate against outsiders.
entries.description: Henri Tajfel's minimal group experiments (1971) showed subjects assigned to meaningless groups (e.g., 'preferred Klee over Kandinsky') still allocated more resources to in-group members and were willing to give up absolute gains to maximize relative advantage. This grew into Social Identity Theory.
entries.example: Sports rivalries, political tribalism, the 'Robbers Cave' experiment (Sherif, 1954). In organizations, team-vs-team budget fights often run hotter than the underlying stakes warrant. Online, arbitrary fandom labels predict harsh treatment of out-group strangers.
entries.howToApply: Notice when 'us vs them' framing kicks in — especially when the group is freshly invented (a new team name, a new product brand). Build superordinate goals that require cross-group cooperation; this reduces bias more reliably than diversity training alone. Personally, name your tribes and ask whether the threat is real.
entries.pitfalls: Some classic studies (Robbers Cave, Stanford Prison) had serious methodological and ethical problems and were partly stage-managed; do not over-cite them. Implicit bias trainings show small, often zero, behavior change in meta-analyses (Forscher et al., 2019), so beware quick fixes.
entries.origin: Henri Tajfel and colleagues, 'Social categorization and intergroup behaviour,' European Journal of Social Psychology (1971).

entries.name: Status Games
entries.oneLiner: Much of human behavior is competition for relative rank — through dominance, prestige, or virtue — not absolute resources.
entries.description: Anthropologists Joseph Henrich and Francisco Gil-White (2001) distinguished two routes to status: dominance (coerced deference) and prestige (freely conferred admiration for skill). Will Storr synthesized this with evolutionary psychology: status motives shape consumption, politics, and online behavior, often unconsciously, because ancestral fitness depended on rank.
entries.example: Luxury goods signal prestige more than they deliver utility (Veblen, 1899). Twitter dunking is a low-cost dominance move; open-sourcing a useful library is a prestige move. Academic citation counts, follower counts, and job titles are status currencies people will trade real money for.
entries.howToApply: Audit which status games you are playing and whether you actually want their prizes (Naval Ravikant's question). Pursue prestige games (skill, generosity, craft) over dominance games where possible — they compound and have positive externalities. Notice when a 'principled' stance is really a status move.
entries.pitfalls: Reducing all behavior to status is itself a status move (signaling cynical sophistication). Some pursuits (love, curiosity, parenting) do not collapse cleanly to rank. Status-blindness is naive; status-obsession corrodes wellbeing — large literatures link relative-rank chasing to anxiety and depression (Wilkinson and Pickett, The Spirit Level, 2009).
entries.origin: Thorstein Veblen, Theory of the Leisure Class (1899); modern dual-route framework: Joseph Henrich and Francisco Gil-White, Evolution and Human Behavior (2001); popularized by Will Storr, The Status Game (2021).

entries.name: Inversion (Invert, Always Invert)
entries.oneLiner: Solve problems backwards by asking what would guarantee failure, then avoid those things.
entries.description: Inversion flips a goal on its head: instead of asking 'how do I succeed?', ask 'what would cause catastrophic failure here?' and systematically eliminate those paths. Munger argues many hard forward problems become tractable when inverted. It pairs well with checklists because failure modes are often more concrete and enumerable than success recipes.
entries.example: Instead of 'how do I have a happy marriage?', ask 'what reliably destroys marriages?' (contempt, financial deceit, neglect) and remove those. Instead of 'how do I get rich?', ask 'how do people go broke?' (leverage, single-stock concentration, lifestyle creep) and avoid them.
entries.howToApply: For any goal, write a second column titled 'How would I guarantee the opposite?'. List 5-10 failure paths, then convert each into a 'do-not-do' rule. Run a quarterly 'how would I sabotage this project?' session before strategy planning.
entries.pitfalls: Inversion identifies what to avoid but not what to pursue — used alone it produces risk-averse, uncreative strategies. Avoidance lists can also become superstition (avoiding things merely correlated with failure). Combine with forward thinking, not as a substitute.
entries.origin: Borrowed by Charlie Munger (Berkshire Hathaway, 1990s-2000s talks, esp. 'A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom,' 1994) from 19th-century mathematician Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi's dictum 'man muss immer umkehren' (invert, always invert).

entries.name: Second-Order Thinking
entries.oneLiner: Ask 'and then what?' — trace the consequences of consequences, not just the first effect.
entries.description: First-order thinking stops at the immediate effect ('rate cuts → stocks up'). Second-order thinking continues: 'if everyone expects that, it's already priced in; the real move depends on whether cuts beat expectations.' Howard Marks argues that consistently outperforming requires this layer because the obvious response is already baked into prices, policies, and crowds.
entries.example: Rent control sounds pro-tenant (first-order) but reduces housing supply and raises prices for new entrants (second-order). 'Just ban X' policies often produce the black market they were meant to eliminate. A startup raising at a sky-high valuation feels like a win until the down-round preference stack wipes out the founders.
entries.howToApply: Before any decision, write three columns: immediate effect, 6-month effect, 3-year effect. For each, ask 'what does everyone else assume, and what happens if they're right vs. wrong?' Reject any thesis that sounds like it would fit on a CNBC chyron — that's first-order.
entries.pitfalls: Easy to spiral into infinite-regress paralysis or to invent clever-sounding contrarian narratives that are simply wrong. Second-order thinking is not 'always do the opposite of the crowd' — sometimes the obvious answer is correct.
entries.origin: Popularized by investor Howard Marks in his Oaktree memos (1990s onward) and the book 'The Most Important Thing' (2011); the underlying idea traces to economist Frédéric Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen.'

entries.name: Opportunity Cost
entries.oneLiner: The true cost of a choice is the best alternative you give up, not just the cash you spend.
entries.description: Every yes is a no to something else. The opportunity cost of a decision is the value of the next-best forgone option — including time, capital, attention, and optionality. Most bad decisions look fine until you price in what was sacrificed (the meeting that displaced deep work, the safe job that displaced the venture).
entries.example: Holding $50k in a 0.5% checking account 'costs' nothing in cash terms, but in a 5% T-bill environment the opportunity cost is ~$2,250/year. Saying yes to a recurring weekly meeting at 9am isn't 'free' — it's the cost of your most productive hour, every week, for a year.
entries.howToApply: When evaluating a yes/no, force-name the alternative: 'If I do X, what specifically am I not doing?' For recurring commitments, multiply by 52 or 12 before agreeing. For money, compare against a baseline yield (T-bill rate) not against zero.
entries.pitfalls: Hyper-optimizing opportunity cost leads to chronic dissatisfaction ('I could always be doing something better'). Some choices have non-quantifiable returns (rest, relationships) that look bad on a spreadsheet but compound over decades.
entries.origin: Coined by Austrian economist Friedrich von Wieser in 'Der natürliche Wert' ('Natural Value,' 1889); the underlying logic of forgone alternatives is implicit in classical economics from Adam Smith (1776) onward.

entries.name: Regret Minimization Framework
entries.oneLiner: Project yourself to age 80 and choose the option you'd least regret not having taken.
entries.description: Bezos used this in 1994 when deciding whether to leave a lucrative Wall Street job to start an internet bookstore. The framework removes short-term loss aversion (bonus, status, sunk effort) by anchoring to a deathbed perspective where most short-term costs become invisible and missed shots loom largest. Best for high-stakes, asymmetric, hard-to-reverse life pivots.
entries.example: Bezos asked: 'When I'm 80, will I regret leaving Wall Street? No. Will I regret missing the beginning of the internet? Yes.' He left and founded Amazon. Modern parallels: leaving a stable job to take a startup founding role, having a child, moving abroad, ending a long but stagnant relationship.
entries.howToApply: Write the decision at the top of a page. Below, write two paragraphs from your 80-year-old self: one if you took the leap, one if you didn't. Choose the path with the smaller regret column. Reserve this tool for decisions whose window genuinely closes — not everyday choices.
entries.pitfalls: Survivorship bias — Bezos worked, but most people who 'followed the dream' did not become billionaires; the framework ignores base rates. It also undervalues stable goods (health, partner, community) whose absence at 80 is the actual regret. Don't apply it to reversible decisions.
entries.origin: Articulated by Jeff Bezos in interviews about his 1994 decision to leave D. E. Shaw and found Amazon; popularized via a 2001 Academy of Achievement interview.

entries.name: Probabilistic Thinking / Expected Value
entries.oneLiner: Multiply each outcome's probability by its payoff, sum them, and pick the highest expected value — judge the bet, not the result.
entries.description: Most real decisions are bets under uncertainty. Expected value (EV) = Σ (probability × outcome). Probabilistic thinking forces you to assign explicit odds, accept that good decisions sometimes lose, and that bad decisions sometimes win ('resulting,' per Annie Duke). Over many decisions, +EV bets compound; over few, variance dominates.
entries.example: A startup job: 10% chance of $5M outcome, 90% chance of $0 = EV $500k, vs. a corporate job at $250k guaranteed. EV favors the startup, but only if you can take many such bets across a career — single-shot, you may prefer the certain payoff. Insurance is a -EV bet you take anyway because the variance (your house burning down once) is unsurvivable.
entries.howToApply: Before a decision, write each outcome and your honest probability (force them to sum to 100%). Compute EV. Then ask: 'Can I survive the worst case? Can I repeat this bet enough for variance to wash out?' Keep a decision journal so you can calibrate your probabilities over time.
entries.pitfalls: Garbage-in probabilities produce false precision — humans are poorly calibrated, especially on tail risks. EV ignores variance and ruin: a +EV bet that has a 1% chance of bankruptcy is still wrong if you only get one shot (Kelly criterion / ergodicity). Don't confuse calculable risk with Knightian uncertainty.
entries.origin: Expected value formalized by Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat in correspondence (1654); modern decision-theoretic form developed by von Neumann and Morgenstern in 'Theory of Games and Economic Behavior' (1944). Popularized for general audiences by Annie Duke ('Thinking in Bets,' 2018).

entries.name: Decision Trees
entries.oneLiner: Map decisions and chance events as a branching tree, assign probabilities and payoffs, and roll back to find the optimal path.
entries.description: A decision tree makes sequential choices under uncertainty visible. Squares are decisions you control, circles are chance nodes, leaves are outcomes with payoffs. You compute expected value at each chance node, then 'fold back' from right to left, pruning dominated branches. Used heavily in clinical decisions, M&A, and operations research.
entries.example: Should you sue, settle, or drop a case? Branch 1: settle for $200k (certain). Branch 2: sue → 60% win $1M, 40% lose -$300k → EV $480k. Tree shows suing has higher EV but higher variance. Or: a doctor weighing surgery vs. watchful waiting given test sensitivity, complication rates, and life expectancy.
entries.howToApply: For any multi-stage decision, draw the tree on paper. Limit to 2-3 levels deep — beyond that, false precision dominates. Run sensitivity analysis: change the probability of each branch by ±20% and see if the recommended action flips. If it does, you need better data before deciding.
entries.pitfalls: Combinatorial explosion — trees become unwieldy fast. Probabilities and payoffs are often guesses dressed as math, producing precise-looking but wrong answers. Ignores option value of waiting and second-order effects. Useless if the real uncertainty is which branches even exist.
entries.origin: Formalized in operations research literature in the 1960s; Howard Raiffa's 'Decision Analysis' (1968) is the canonical text. Roots in statistical decision theory (Wald, 1950) and game-tree analysis.

entries.name: OODA Loop
entries.oneLiner: Observe, Orient, Decide, Act — and cycle faster than your opponent to stay inside their decision loop.
entries.description: Boyd's insight from air combat: victory often goes not to the better-equipped pilot but to the one whose decision cycle is faster, because by the time the opponent reorients, the situation has already changed again. 'Orient' is the heaviest step — it filters reality through mental models, culture, and prior experience, and is where most decisions silently go wrong.
entries.example: A startup shipping weekly while incumbents ship quarterly is operating inside their OODA loop — by the time the incumbent responds, the startup has moved on. In a crisis (PR, outage, market crash), the team that publishes a coherent response in 2 hours dominates the narrative vs. the one whose lawyers are still drafting at hour 24.
entries.howToApply: In any competitive or fast-changing situation, optimize Orient first: kill stale assumptions, get raw data not summaries, and shorten the loop between observation and action. Time-box decisions ('we decide by Friday with what we know'). Reserve slow, high-quality loops for irreversible calls.
entries.pitfalls: Speed worship — fast loops on the wrong frame just get you to the wrong place faster. Boyd himself emphasized Orient as primary, but pop versions reduce OODA to 'be fast,' which justifies thoughtless action. Not appropriate for irreversible, low-urgency decisions where deliberation dominates.
entries.origin: Developed by U.S. Air Force Colonel John Boyd in the 1970s-80s, drawn from his analysis of Korean War air combat (F-86 vs. MiG-15) and presented in his briefing 'Patterns of Conflict' (1986); never published as a book in his lifetime.

entries.name: Pre-mortem
entries.oneLiner: Before launching, imagine the project has failed catastrophically and write the autopsy — then fix what you found.
entries.description: Klein's pre-mortem inverts a post-mortem: the team is told 'it's one year from now, this project failed spectacularly — write down why.' Prospective hindsight (imagining a definite outcome) increases the ability to identify reasons for future outcomes by ~30% (Mitchell, Russo, & Pennington, 1989). It also creates psychological safety for dissenters who'd otherwise stay silent.
entries.example: Before a product launch, the team writes individual one-pagers: 'It's Q4. The launch failed. What killed us?' Common findings: 'We assumed enterprise sales cycles were 30 days, they were 9 months,' 'Our biggest customer churned because the migration broke their integrations.' These get added to the risk register with owners.
entries.howToApply: 10 minutes before any kickoff, have each team member silently write 3 reasons the project failed in 12 months, then share. Cluster, rank by probability × impact, and assign one mitigation owner per top-5 risk. Re-run quarterly; treat new failure modes as updates, not noise.
entries.pitfalls: Becomes theater if leadership has already committed publicly — people self-censor 'real' risks. Can produce a long list with no follow-through. Doesn't catch unknown unknowns; it surfaces what the team can already imagine. Klein's claim of +30% generation rests on a single 1989 study; treat the magnitude as suggestive, not settled.
entries.origin: Coined by cognitive psychologist Gary Klein, 'Performing a Project Premortem,' Harvard Business Review (September 2007). Builds on Mitchell, Russo & Pennington's research on prospective hindsight (Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 1989).

entries.name: Reversible vs. Irreversible Decisions (Two-Way vs. One-Way Doors)
entries.oneLiner: Reversible decisions deserve speed; irreversible ones deserve deliberation — and most decisions are reversible.
entries.description: Bezos divides decisions into Type 2 ('two-way doors' — you can walk back through if it doesn't work) and Type 1 ('one-way doors' — you cannot undo). The fatal mistake at scale is using the heavyweight Type 1 process on Type 2 decisions, which produces slowness, risk-aversion, and decline. Most personal and organizational decisions are two-way doors mistakenly treated as one-way.
entries.example: Two-way doors: trying a new tool for a quarter, taking a job (you can quit), launching a feature (you can roll back), moving cities. One-way doors: having a child, selling your company, public accusations, tattoos, posting a permanent statement, taking on non-dischargeable debt.
entries.howToApply: Before deliberating, label the decision: 'If this is wrong, what does it cost to reverse?' If reversible in <90 days for <10% of stakes, decide today with 70% information (Bezos's heuristic). If genuinely irreversible, slow down, gather more data, and seek disconfirming evidence — but then commit.
entries.pitfalls: People over-classify decisions as irreversible (status quo bias). Conversely, some 'reversible' decisions have hidden lock-in (switching costs, reputation damage, data lock-in). Speed on a Type 2 only helps if you actually reverse when it's wrong — many teams keep going out of sunk-cost commitment.
entries.origin: Articulated by Jeff Bezos in Amazon's 2015 and 2016 Letters to Shareholders ('Day 1' framing); the underlying option-theory intuition predates him in real options analysis (Dixit & Pindyck, 'Investment Under Uncertainty,' 1994).

entries.name: 10-10-10 Rule
entries.oneLiner: Ask how you'll feel about this decision in 10 minutes, 10 months, and 10 years to neutralize emotional distortion.
entries.description: Welch's heuristic forces you to evaluate a decision across three time horizons simultaneously. The 10-minute horizon honors immediate emotion; 10 months captures medium-term consequences (career, finances, relationships); 10 years captures whether it matters at all in the arc of your life. Most heated decisions look very different across these three lenses, and the discrepancy reveals what's actually at stake.
entries.example: Sending an angry email to a colleague: 10 min — cathartic; 10 months — awkward 1:1s and a damaged reference; 10 years — possibly a closed door at a future company. Or: skipping a friend's wedding to finish a deck. 10 min — relief; 10 months — strained friendship; 10 years — you'll remember the wedding, not the deck.
entries.howToApply: When you feel a decision pulling on you emotionally, literally write three lines on paper labeled 10m / 10mo / 10yr and answer each. If the 10-year answer is 'won't matter,' stop overthinking. If 10-month and 10-year answers conflict with the 10-minute pull, the 10-minute pull is almost always the one to discount.
entries.pitfalls: Long horizons can rationalize chronic self-denial ('it won't matter in 10 years' applied to every joy). Some decisions genuinely are about the next 10 minutes (acute pain, safety) and the long view distorts them. The framework is folk wisdom, not validated psychology — treat it as a prompt for reflection, not a proof.
entries.origin: Suzy Welch, '10-10-10: A Fast and Powerful Way to Get Unstuck in Love, at Work, and with Your Family' (Scribner, 2009); Welch first wrote about it in O, The Oprah Magazine in 2006.
